title: The Dhammapada in the world
hookLine: carried across Asia in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit and Chinese; Max Müller brought it into English in 1870

cards: In the eighteen nineties, in the desert near Khotan, on the old Silk Road in what is now western China, a French expedition came away with pieces of a very old manuscript.
Birch bark, in a script few people could read, in a language of the old northwest of India. When scholars finally worked it out, they found verses they knew.
Far from where the Pali canon was kept, someone had carried the same sayings you've been reading.

teach.b: The version you've read is the Pali Dhammapada, kept by the Theravada tradition of Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia. But it has cousins.
That birch-bark manuscript is the Gandhari Dharmapada, named after Gandhara, the region of today's northern Pakistan and eastern Afghanistan where its language was spoken.
Another version survives in a mixed Indian language and is named after the city of Patna.
A larger Sanskrit collection, the Udanavarga, used by other early schools, shares many verses with it and was later translated into Tibetan.

And the sayings went into Chinese early, in the third century, and were read in monasteries. The collections don't match exactly: chapters are arranged differently, some verses are missing, some are added.
What's striking is how much stays the same across languages and centuries: hatred ending by not-hatred, the mind coming first, the bee and the flower.
Then the verses traveled west. A Danish scholar, Viggo Fausböll, published the Pali text in Europe with a Latin translation in the eighteen fifties.
Max Müller brought it into English in eighteen seventy and revised it in eighteen eighty-one for the Sacred Books of the East, the version you've read.
Many more translations have followed, and the book is still read by Buddhists and by people of other paths.
Each of them carried it: monks memorizing on foot, scribes on birch bark, translators at desks. And now you, if you pass one verse along.

how: The Pali Dhammapada is chanted and studied throughout Theravada Buddhism; related collections were kept by other early schools, and Tibetan and East Asian Buddhists know the sayings through the Udanavarga and Chinese versions.

games.q: you're a scholar in the 1890s, holding birch bark in a script few people can read. what do you do?
o: work at the script until it speaks.
throw it out; it's too damaged.
games.why: scholars worked it out, and found Dhammapada verses carried far from the Pali canon.

practice: Picture the long line of people who carried these verses to you: a monk walking a mountain road, reciting under his breath; a scribe in Gandhara, writing on bark; a translator in China, searching for the right word; a scholar in Oxford with his lamp.
Then you, here. Hold one verse from your ten, and think of one person who might like to hear it; you're next in the line.

wordCard.voice: Gandhari Dharmapada. A birch-bark manuscript found near Khotan, a cousin of the Pali text: the sayings were carried in Pali, Gandhari, Sanskrit, Chinese and Tibetan, then into English in eighteen seventy.

orig.note: Pali dhammapada; in Gandhari and Sanskrit the same title is dharmapada.

carryVoice: Your line: who else carried it. A long line of hands, and now yours. Day two hundred thirty, done.
